subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A 34-year-old man presents to the emergency department 30 minutes after eating tuna at a seafood buffet. He has no known drug or food allergies. He is afebrile with blood pressure 105/65 mm Hg, heart rate 96/min, and respiratory rate 18/min. Examination shows marked facial flushing, oral burning, diffuse erythema, and urticaria. Bronchospasm is not present.
question: Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this patient's symptoms?

options.text: Bacterial conversion of histidine to histamine in spoiled fish
Opening of fast voltage-gated sodium channels in nerve tissue
IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation triggered by fish protein
Binding and total block of fast voltage-gated sodium channels
Accumulation of a heat-stable toxin in large predatory reef fish

explanation_correct: This presentation is classic for scombroid (histamine) poisoning. Spoiled dark-meat fish such as tuna, mahi-mahi, mackerel, and bonito contain bacteria with histidine decarboxylase that converts fish histidine to histamine. Ingestion of the preformed histamine produces flushing, oral burning, erythema, urticaria, and itching that frequently mimics fish allergy or anaphylaxis, even in patients without a prior allergic history.

explanation_incorrect.B: Opening of sodium channels causing depolarization is the action of ciguatoxin, found in reef fish such as barracuda and snapper; it produces gastrointestinal symptoms, perioral numbness, and hot-cold sensation reversal rather than urticaria and flushing.
explanation_incorrect.C: Scombroid poisoning is not a true IgE-mediated allergy; the histamine is preformed in the spoiled fish by bacterial decarboxylation, which is why it is frequently misdiagnosed as fish allergy.
explanation_incorrect.D: Total block of fast voltage-gated sodium channels is the action of tetrodotoxin from pufferfish, causing nausea, paresthesias, weakness, and loss of reflexes without histamine-mediated skin findings.
explanation_incorrect.E: Heat-stable toxin accumulation in predatory reef fish describes ciguatoxin poisoning, which presents with vomiting, diarrhea, perioral numbness, and reversal of hot and cold sensations rather than urticaria and flushing.

educationalObjective: Scombroid poisoning results from bacterial histidine decarboxylase converting histidine to histamine in spoiled dark-meat fish and classically mimics fish allergy.

subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A 42-year-old man develops nausea, diarrhea, and perioral paresthesias several hours after eating sashimi prepared from pufferfish. On examination he is afebrile with diffuse weakness, dizziness, and markedly diminished deep tendon reflexes. His pupils are equal and reactive, the skin shows no urticaria or flushing, and he is hemodynamically stable. His physician notes that no specific pharmacologic antidote exists.
question: Which of the following toxin actions best explains this patient's findings?

options.text: Bacterial decarboxylation of histidine in inadequately refrigerated fish
Opening of neuronal sodium channels causing sustained depolarization
Binding of fast voltage-gated sodium channels, preventing depolarization
Irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase at neuromuscular junctions
Histamine release producing bronchospasm and angioedema

explanation_correct: Tetrodotoxin from pufferfish binds fast voltage-gated sodium channels in nerve tissue, preventing depolarization. This produces nausea, diarrhea, paresthesias, weakness, dizziness, and loss of reflexes. Treatment is supportive because no antidote exists.

explanation_incorrect.A: Bacterial histidine decarboxylation causes scombroid poisoning, which produces flushing, urticaria, and oral burning mimicking anaphylaxis rather than weakness and loss of reflexes.
explanation_incorrect.B: Opening sodium channels and causing depolarization is the action of ciguatoxin from reef fish, associated with hot-cold sensation reversal, bradycardia, and heart block, not loss of reflexes from blocked conduction.
explanation_incorrect.D: Acetylcholinesterase inhibition (organophosphate poisoning) causes a cholinergic crisis with salivation, lacrimation, miosis, and bronchospasm; tetrodotoxin acts directly on sodium channels, not on the enzyme.
explanation_incorrect.E: Histamine-mediated symptoms such as bronchospasm and angioedema occur in scombroid poisoning; the absence of urticaria and flushing in this patient argues against a histamine-driven process.

educationalObjective: Tetrodotoxin from pufferfish blocks fast voltage-gated sodium channels in nerve tissue, preventing depolarization; treatment is supportive.

subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A 51-year-old woman is evaluated for vomiting, diarrhea, and perioral numbness that began 6 hours after eating a barracuda caught during a fishing trip. She reports that the hot coffee she was drinking felt oddly cold while the ice water felt hot. Heart rate is 48/min, blood pressure is 92/60 mm Hg, and the skin is without urticaria. ECG shows no atrioventricular block on this tracing.
question: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

options.text: Histamine accumulation from bacterial contamination of the fish
Tetrodotoxin blockade of fast voltage-gated sodium channels
Ciguatoxin opening sodium channels and causing depolarization
Anticholinergic toxin causing mydriasis and urinary retention
Preformed toxin requiring antihistamine and epinephrine therapy

explanation_correct: Reef fish such as barracuda, snapper, and moray eel harbor ciguatoxin, which opens sodium channels and causes depolarization. Classic findings are nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, perioral numbness, reversal of hot and cold sensations, and bradycardia, heart block, or hypotension. Treatment is supportive.

explanation_incorrect.A: Histamine accumulation (scombroid) occurs in spoiled dark-meat fish such as tuna and mackerel and causes flushing, urticaria, and oral burning; hot-cold reversal is not a feature.
explanation_incorrect.B: Tetrodotoxin blocks sodium channels, preventing depolarization, and is associated with pufferfish ingestion, producing weakness and loss of reflexes rather than reversal of temperature sensation.
explanation_incorrect.D: An anticholinergic toxin would produce mydriasis, dry skin, urinary retention, and delirium; this patient has perioral numbness and bradycardia, which do not fit that syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.E: Antihistamines and epinephrine are treatments for scombroid histamine poisoning; ciguatoxin has no antidote and is managed supportively.

educationalObjective: Ciguatoxin from reef fish opens sodium channels causing depolarization; reversal of hot and cold sensations is the classic clue.

subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A 29-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 20 minutes after eating spoiled mahi-mahi. He has facial flushing, diffuse urticaria, oral burning, and wheezing on auscultation. Blood pressure is 84/50 mm Hg, heart rate is 112/min, and oxygen saturation is 92% on room air. The team is preparing immediate management for his reaction.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: 100% oxygen with consideration of hyperbaric oxygen therapy
Antihistamines, with albuterol and epinephrine if severe
Atropine followed by pralidoxime
Sodium bicarbonate to stabilize cardiac cell membranes
Supportive care alone, as no specific therapy exists

explanation_correct: Scombroid poisoning from spoiled dark-meat fish (eg, tuna, mahi-mahi, mackerel, bonito) delivers preformed histamine and mimics anaphylaxis, progressing in severe cases to bronchospasm, angioedema, and hypotension. Treatment is antihistamines, with albuterol and/or epinephrine added for severe bronchospasm and hypotension.

explanation_incorrect.A: 100% and hyperbaric oxygen are treatments for carbon monoxide poisoning; they do nothing for histamine-mediated bronchospasm and hypotension.
explanation_incorrect.C: Atropine followed by pralidoxime treats poisoning by acetylcholinesterase inhibitors and organophosphates, which cause salivation, miosis, and bronchorrhea rather than urticaria and flushing.
explanation_incorrect.D: Sodium bicarbonate stabilizes cardiac membranes in tricyclic antidepressant overdose and alkalinizes the urine in salicylate toxicity; it has no role in histamine poisoning.
explanation_incorrect.E: Supportive care alone is the management of tetrodotoxin and ciguatoxin poisoning, but scombroid poisoning has specific therapy — antihistamines — so this patient should not be managed supportively alone.

educationalObjective: Severe scombroid poisoning is treated with antihistamines, with albuterol and epinephrine added for bronchospasm and hypotension.
